name: Bilal Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good morning, Bilal, and thank you for your time. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or the government, and nothing you say will carry your name. You can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think in private.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Good morning. I'm happy to help, as long as it's not going in the newspaper with my face. I'm a simple man, I'll just tell you how my life is.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: That's what I'd like to hear. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up for prayer before five, then I drive to the Northgate business park, where we're building industrial units for a regional contractor. I'm a labourer and carpenter's mate, so I build the timber shuttering for the concrete bases, put up the site fencing, carry and clean. I ran my father's corner shop for twenty years until the big supermarket opened on the bypass, so I'm only four years in this trade and still slow. I like that you can see what you did at the end of the day, and that nobody can argue with a straight wall. What wears me out is the cold in my hands in winter, and the young site manager who talks to me like I'm a schoolboy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the world still needs men who work with their hands. I'd say it at the mosque after Friday prayers, where the men always ask each other about work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved. I'm not clever with computers and I don't want to be. I want to learn the trade properly and provide for my family, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, every day, the same. Ask the foreman if he'll teach me more of the carpentry, maybe the formwork for the stairs. Put a little away if I can, but there is rarely anything left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, thank God. This is how life should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the shop. What happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father opened it in 1989 and I took it over when he got sick. Then the supermarket came, with longer hours and cheaper prices, and in two years we went from busy to empty. I closed it myself, I locked the door and cried in the car, and then I went to find work the next week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does money work at home at the moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia is at home with the children and does sewing alterations for neighbours, a little money. My wage pays the mortgage and the food and not much more. We have maybe two weeks of money in the bank, and if something big comes, my brother Kamran helps, and I help him when I can.

S0.say: Good, the world still needs men who work with their hands. I'd say it at the mosque after Friday prayers, when the men ask each other about work.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, because I'm not clever with computers and I don't want to be. I want to learn the trade properly and provide for my family, that's all.
S0.do: Keeps going every day as before and asks the foreman to teach him more carpentry, such as formwork for stairs. Tries to put a little away, though there is rarely anything left.
S0.feel: Calm and thankful that life goes on as it should.
S0.quote: I closed it myself, I locked the door and cried in the car, and then I went to find work the next week.
S0.fieldNote: He has already lost a family business to bigger competition and responded by finding work the very next week, which says a lot about his values. His faith and his community at the mosque are central to how he talks about work. Family, not the state, is his safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a man has to work harder and adapt, that's life. My father came here with nothing and he never asked anyone for a handout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm a bit worried. The young ones on site pick up new things fast, and I'm slow. If machines take some of the jobs, I'm afraid the foreman will keep the young ones and let the slow ones go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep my head down, work harder so they see I'm reliable. Cut back at home where we can. I wouldn't go near the computers, I'd just try to be the man they can trust to turn up every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like there's a cloud over the site, not raining yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame when changes like this happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies who only care about money, and the government with all its rules that make small men's lives hard. Not the machine, the machine is just a machine. It's the people at the top who don't know what it is to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back on, if things got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car is old, so we'd keep it running ourselves, no new one. Less meat in the week, more lentils, which Nadia says is healthier anyway. And we'd stop the children's after-school tutoring, which hurts me, because I want them to do better than me.

S1.say: A man has to work harder and adapt, that's life. My father came here with nothing and never asked anyone for a handout.
S1.think: I'm a bit worried, because the young ones on site pick up new things fast and I'm slow. If machines take some jobs, the foreman will keep the young ones and let the slow ones go.
S1.do: Keeps working and keeps his head down, trying to prove himself as the most reliable man on site. Cuts back at home on meat, a new car and the children's after-school tutoring, and stays away from computers.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a cloud over the site that hasn't started raining.
S1.quote: It's the people at the top who don't know what it is to work.
S1.fieldNote: His answer to change is to be the most reliable man on site, not to learn new technology. He blames big companies and government rules rather than the machines. Cutting his children's tutoring was the sacrifice that hurt him most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is madness, and the people in charge have lost their minds. Who decided this? Nobody asked the working man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm frightened. If robots can do the building work in two years, what is left for a man like me? I'm forty-three, no schooling, no computer skills, and no other building work near home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut everything we can straight away. Talk to Kamran about putting our families together under one roof, so we only pay one mortgage. Ask at the mosque if there's any work or help, because the community looks after its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the shop all over again, only worse, because then I had my strength and my years. Now I'm older and there's nothing to run to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change for you, compared with a slower picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is no time to learn something new, even if I wanted to. With a slower picture, maybe I could work until the children are older. With two years, Sami is fifteen and Aisha is twelve, they still need everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you turn first for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, always. Kamran, then my cousins, then the mosque. I would not want government money unless there was no other way, because I believe a man should support his family, but I wouldn't let my children go hungry for my pride.

S2.say: This is madness, and the people in charge have lost their minds. Who decided this? Nobody asked the working man.
S2.think: I'm frightened. If robots can do building work in two years, what is left for a man of forty-three with no schooling, no computer skills and no other building work near home?
S2.do: Cuts spending straight away and talks to his brother Kamran about combining their families under one roof to pay only one mortgage. Asks the mosque community for work or help, and turns to government aid only as a last resort.
S2.feel: Like losing the shop all over again but worse, because he's older and has nothing to run to.
S2.quote: Like the shop all over again, only worse, because then I had my strength and my years.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture brings back the pain of losing his father's shop. His plan rests on family and faith community, and he is clear that state help is a last resort. His pride gives way only when he thinks of his children going hungry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, so families should prepare and people should stop wasting money. I'd say the government should get out of the way and let businesses create new jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's still very bad for me. Five years is more time, but I'm still slow and still bad with computers. I'd just be watching it come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save every penny I can, maybe fifty a month, and cut back on everything else. Keep working as long as they'll keep me. Talk to Kamran now about what we'd do, so we have a plan before it comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Like carrying a bag of cement that gets a little heavier each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years of warning, what would you do while you see it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every month a little in the bank, no holidays, no eating out, Nadia sewing more. I'd try to pay off the small debts so we don't owe anyone. We'd teach the children that money must be respected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning to work with the new machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if someone showed me in person, but I don't think I'd be good at it. My son Sami helps me with my phone. I'd rather he learns it properly and I keep doing what I know.

S3.say: Five years is a warning, so families should prepare and stop wasting money. The government should get out of the way and let businesses create new jobs.
S3.think: It's still very bad for me. Five years is more time, but I'm still slow and still bad with computers, so I'd just be watching it come.
S3.do: Saves about 50 a month by cutting holidays and eating out, and pays off small debts. Keeps working as long as he's wanted and makes a plan with his brother Kamran before it arrives.
S3.feel: Heavy, like carrying a bag of cement that gets heavier every year.
S3.quote: Like carrying a bag of cement that gets a little heavier each year.
S3.fieldNote: Five years doesn't change much for him because he doesn't see himself learning new skills. He wants the government to step back and let businesses create jobs, while still planning to lean on his family. He'd rather his son learn the technology than learn it himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for people to prepare, if they work hard and look after their families. No need to cry about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it feels better. In ten years the children are grown, the mortgage is smaller, and I'd have saved a little. But I'd still be a man with only his hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, save what I can, and push Sami towards a good apprenticeship, maybe in electrics or fixing machines. Help Aisha with her studies so she can go further than me. Keep going with my work until the day they don't need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but less. With God's help and my family, I think we'd manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be fifty-three by 2036. Does ten years feel different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is the difference between my children being children and my children being adults. If they're grown, I can live on less. A man and his wife can manage on little, it's the children you worry for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Sami and Aisha?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want Sami to have a trade, a real one that the machines need people for, like electrics or repairs. And Aisha, she's clever, maybe a teacher or a nurse. Jobs with people, jobs with respect.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time for people to prepare, if they work hard and look after their families. There's no need to cry about it.
S4.think: It feels better, with the children grown, the mortgage smaller and a little saved. But I'd still be a man with only his hands.
S4.do: Keeps working and saves what he can while steering his son towards an apprenticeship in electrics or machine repair. Helps his daughter with her studies so she can go further than him.
S4.feel: Less worried, trusting that with God's help and his family they would manage.
S4.quote: A man and his wife can manage on little, it's the children you worry for.
S4.fieldNote: The ten-year picture eases him mainly because his children would be grown. He pours his hopes into apprenticeships and respected work for them, in line with his traditional values. His faith gives him a steadiness that is not the same as feeling safe.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my children would still be young and there's no time for anything. What would help is real apprenticeships, for older men too, where you learn on the job and get paid. Not handouts, work. And for the companies to remember that people need jobs to feed families.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about dignity. A man who works feels like a man. If you take away the work and give him a cheque, maybe he eats, but something inside him dies.

headlineQuote: If you take away the work and give him a cheque, maybe he eats, but something inside him dies.
portrait: Bilal is a 43-year-old labourer and carpenter's mate on a business park build, who came to construction after a supermarket put his father's corner shop out of business. A man of faith with a wife and two children, he has about two weeks of savings and relies on his brother and the mosque community when money runs short. He avoids computers and plans to survive change by being the most reliable worker on site. He is calm in the plateau, uneasy in the steady picture and alarmed by the faster AGI pictures, easing only when ten years would let his children grow up. He blames big companies and government rules and wants work and apprenticeships, not handouts.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because his children would still be young and there would be no time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: Real paid apprenticeships, including for older men, where people learn on the job, and companies remembering that people need work to feed their families.
